blocks.text: Keep two ideas apart. **Cholestasis** is a _biochemical_ state: impaired bile flow raises ALP, serum bile acids and bilirubin. **Biliary disease** is _structural_ pathology anywhere from the small intrahepatic ducts down to the sphincter of Oddi. They usually travel together, but either can occur alone, e.g. pure drug-induced cholestasis with normal ducts, or a duct lesion that does not yet impede bile flow.

blocks.title: Main groups of biliary tract disease
rows: Silent stones, biliary pain, acute and chronic cholecystitis, bile duct stones (choledocholithiasis), cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
Commonest biliary disorder; a diseased gallbladder without stones is unusual
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), IgG4-associated cholangitis
Chronic cholestasis that may end in biliary cirrhosis
Secondary sclerosing cholangitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis
Follows long-standing large-duct obstruction, surgery or infection
Recurrent cholangitis and a raised cholangiocarcinoma risk
Gallbladder carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, ampullary carcinoma; gallbladder polyps
Cholangiocarcinoma usually presents with obstructive jaundice; gallbladder cancer with biliary pain, then jaundice; polyps are mostly incidental
Biliary-type pain; sphincterotomy helps organic stenosis (and high pressures on manometry), not functional pain

blocks.title: Gallstone types
rows: More than half cholesterol; the large majority of stones in Western countries (about 80-85%)
Female, older age, obesity, pregnancy, rapid weight loss
Chronic haemolysis, cirrhosis, older age, ileal disease or resection
Calcium bilirubinate crystals, soft and crumbly
Infected bile and stasis (bacteria, parasites); common in the Far East; can form in the ducts

blocks.title: PBC versus PSC at a glance (Davidson)
rows: Sjogren's, other autoimmune and thyroid disease

items: **Type I** - diffuse dilatation of the common bile duct (CBD), about 87%
**Type II** - diverticulum of the duct (7%); **Type III** - intraduodenal dilatation (3%)
**Type IV** - multiple cysts (3%); merges with Caroli's disease
Adults get recurrent pain, jaundice and cholangitis; cholangiocarcinoma risk is raised, so the cyst is excised with a hepatico-jejunostomy
blocks.title: Choledochal cysts (cystic dilatation anywhere in the biliary tree)

blocks.text: Most gallstones (about 80%) never cause symptoms. When gallbladder disease is found, think of stones first - disease without stones is the exception.
Do not equate 'cholestasis' with 'obstruction'. Raised ALP and bilirubin with **normal, undilated ducts** points to intrahepatic causes (drugs, PBC, sepsis) rather than a stone in the CBD.

blocks.title: Cholesterol stones: three mechanisms
rows: Older age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss
Fasting, total parenteral nutrition, spinal cord injury, pregnancy
Pregnancy; bile salt loss from ileal disease or resection
Family history, multiparity, diabetes, octreotide-treated acromegaly, oestrogen/oral contraceptive pill

items: **Black** - haemolysis (e.g. hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease), cirrhosis, ileal disease, older age

**Brown** - bacterial or parasitic infection of bile with stasis; bacterial enzymes free bilirubin, which precipitates with calcium; typical of the Far East and of strictured or post-cholecystectomy ducts
blocks.title: Pigment stones

items: **Acute cholecystitis** - almost always a stone blocking the gallbladder neck or cystic duct; rarely mucus, worms, tumour or a bile duct stent. Early inflammation is chemical: about half of gallbladder cultures are sterile at surgery
**Acalculous cholecystitis** - critically ill patients (ICU, major surgery, sepsis, burns, trauma), parenteral nutrition, sickle cell disease, diabetes
**Acute cholangitis** - bacterial infection above an obstruction: duct stones (the majority, about 85%), benign or malignant strictures, tumours, stents, or after ERCP; liver flukes in endemic areas

**Choledocholithiasis** - in 10-15% of people with gallstones; most stones have migrated from the gallbladder. Primary duct stones in the Far East follow infection with _Clonorchis sinensis_, _Ascaris lumbricoides_ or _Fasciola hepatica_
blocks.title: Gallbladder and duct inflammation

blocks.text: **PBC** is autoimmune: antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) is directed against the **pyruvate dehydrogenase complex**, there is an HLA-DR8 association, and granulomatous inflammation destroys the interlobular bile ducts, leading in time to fibrosis and cirrhosis. It is commoner in women (about 9:1), in northern Europe and North America, and in smokers; clustering suggests an environmental trigger in a genetically susceptible host.

**PSC** has an unknown cause but a close link with inflammatory bowel disease: about **two-thirds** of patients have ulcerative colitis, and 3-10% of people with ulcerative colitis (especially extensive colitis) develop PSC; the rate in Crohn's colitis is about 1%. The HLA A1-B8-DR3 haplotype is associated.

items: Previous bile duct surgery with stricturing; bile duct stones with cholangitis
Intrahepatic 5-fluorodeoxyuridine infusion; formalin injected into hydatid cysts; alcohol injected into tumours
Parasites such as _Clonorchis_
IgG4-associated cholangitis / autoimmune pancreatitis
AIDS (probably cytomegalovirus or _Cryptosporidium_)
blocks.title: Causes of secondary sclerosing cholangitis

blocks.text: Secondary biliary cirrhosis needs months of large-duct blockage (stones, benign strictures, sclerosing cholangitis). Carcinomas rarely cause it because patients seldom live long enough.

Books quote different UC figures for PSC (about two-thirds in Davidson; 70% to over 75% in quick sources). For the exam use Davidson: roughly **two in three** PSC patients have UC, but only a small minority (3-10%) of UC patients get PSC.

items: Sudden onset, steady (not waxing and waning) and lasting about 2 hours
Felt in the epigastrium (70%) or right upper quadrant (20%); radiates to the interscapular area or the tip of the right scapula
Can mimic myocardial infarction, oesophagitis or aortic dissection
Pain continuing beyond **6 hours** suggests a complication - cholecystitis or pancreatitis
No fever, leucocytosis or peritonism; examination is often normal
blocks.title: Biliary pain ('biliary colic')
Telling the three gallstone syndromes apart

items: RUQ pain spreading to the shoulder tip or interscapular region, with fever and leucocytosis
**Murphy's sign**: tenderness and catching of breath on inspiration under the right costal margin
Perforation in 10-15%; empyema may form; gas-forming (emphysematous) infection in the elderly and diabetic
In old age signs may be few, and empyema and perforation are more frequent
blocks.title: Acute cholecystitis

items: **Charcot's triad**: jaundice, fever (with or without rigors) and RUQ pain - present in only about 70% or fewer
**Reynolds' pentad** adds shock and confusion (about 15% of patients)
Jaundice with duct stones **fluctuates** and is nearly always preceded by pain; steadily deepening painless jaundice suggests cancer
Elderly or immunosuppressed patients may present only with confusion, malaise or abnormal LFTs
blocks.title: Bile duct stones and cholangitis

items: Mucocele and **empyema** of the gallbladder; **porcelain gallbladder** (calcified wall)
Choledocholithiasis, cholangitis and acute pancreatitis
**Mirizzi's syndrome** - a stone impacted in the cystic duct compresses or strictures the common hepatic duct, giving obstructive jaundice; the main differential is a malignant stricture
Cholecysto-enteric fistula (air in the biliary tree) and **gallstone ileus** - a stone over 2.5 cm impacts, usually at the terminal ileum
Carcinoma of the gallbladder
blocks.title: Complications of gallstones

items: Early: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, itch
Late: poor absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), so weight loss, fatty stools, osteomalacia and easy bleeding; xanthelasma and xanthomas
Stigmata of chronic liver disease are absent in pure extrahepatic obstruction
blocks.title: Features of cholestatic jaundice

blocks.text: **Courvoisier's law**: a palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient makes gallstone obstruction unlikely (a chronically inflamed, stone-filled gallbladder cannot distend) and suggests malignant obstruction such as pancreatic cancer.

'Colic' is a misnomer - biliary pain is constant. Also, fatty food intolerance, bloating and flatulence are **not** caused by gallstones; treat them as functional dyspepsia rather than an indication for cholecystectomy.

sections.title: Clinical features of PBC, PSC and biliary tumours

items: Often found on routine bloods (raised ALP) in a woman over 30
Fatigue and **pruritus** (often worst on the limbs) precede jaundice by months or years; jaundice is a late feature
Fever and rigors do **not** occur
Xanthelasma/xanthomas, hepatomegaly, later splenomegaly as portal hypertension develops
Bone disease: osteoporosis common, osteomalacia rare
Associations: sicca (Sjogren's) syndrome, systemic sclerosis, coeliac disease and thyroid disease - check thyroid function in a tired patient
blocks.title: Primary biliary cholangitis

items: Classically a persistently raised ALP in a young man with ulcerative colitis
Fatigue, intermittent jaundice, weight loss, RUQ pain and itch
Acute bacterial cholangitis is uncommon unless the ducts have been instrumented
Cholangiocarcinoma develops in about 10-30% over the disease course (lifetime about 20%)
Patients with PSC plus UC have a higher colorectal neoplasia risk than UC alone
blocks.title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis

blocks.text: **IgG4-associated cholangitis** often presents with obstructive jaundice from hilar or low bile duct strictures. Its cholangiogram can look like PSC or hilar cholangiocarcinoma, but over 90% have autoimmune pancreatitis, serum IgG4 is often raised, and - unlike PSC - it responds well to glucocorticoids.

blocks.title: Biliary tumours
rows: Hilar 50-60%, intrahepatic 20-25%, distal CBD 20%. Risks: gallstones, primary or secondary sclerosing cholangitis, Caroli's disease, choledochal cysts, liver flukes (_Clonorchis_)
Obstructive (often painless) jaundice; about half have pain and weight loss
Older women (usually over 70); adenocarcinoma in over 90%; gallstones present in 70-80%; porcelain gallbladder and polyps over 1 cm are high risk
Biliary pain, then persistent jaundice and weight loss; may be a palpable mass; sometimes found incidentally at cholecystectomy (1-3% of removed gallbladders)

blocks.text: Cholangiocarcinoma risk in PSC varies between books (Davidson 10-30%, about 20% lifetime; Kumar and quick sources up to 15-20%). Use Davidson's figures, and remember that a new **dominant stricture** in PSC must be treated as possible cholangiocarcinoma.

Davidson treats gallstones as a key cause of gallbladder cancer (stones in 70-80% of cases), whereas Kumar calls the link unproven. For exams, gallstones (and porcelain gallbladder) are the main risk factors.

items: Start with LFTs, urine for bilirubin and liver ultrasound
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with **dilated ducts** = obstructive jaundice - go on to cholangiography (MRCP or ERCP)
Abnormal LFTs with no biliary dilatation = hepatocellular or intrahepatic cholestasis - serology, immunoglobulins, autoantibodies
A prolonged PT from vitamin K malabsorption corrects with vitamin K; one due to liver failure does not
blocks.title: Work-up of jaundice
Imaging the biliary tree
rows: First-line: gallstones, duct dilatation, gallbladder wall
Non-invasive cholangiogram as good as ERCP; key test for PSC; for possible duct stones without jaundice or sepsis
Mainly **therapeutic**: sphincterotomy, stone extraction, stenting, brushings; risks post-ERCP pancreatitis
Very accurate for duct stones and microlithiasis (recurrent unexplained pancreatitis); no pancreatitis risk from cannulation
When ultrasound is equivocal for acute cholecystitis: non-filling of the gallbladder supports the diagnosis; a normal scan excludes it
Drainage when the duct cannot be reached endoscopically

items: Cholecystitis: leucocytosis (may be absent in the elderly), slight rises in transaminases and amylase
Always check amylase; only a level **above 1000 U/L** confidently pins the pain on acute pancreatitis
Plain chest and abdominal films help exclude basal pneumonia and a perforated viscus
Duct stones: bilirubin above 200 umol/L almost always means complete obstruction; transaminases can briefly reach 10-15x normal (ALT > AST), mimicking hepatitis
Cholangitis: blood cultures positive in about 30% (E. coli, _Enterococcus faecalis_, anaerobes)
blocks.title: Blood tests in gallstone disease

items: **PBC**: cholestatic LFTs, raised IgM and cholesterol, positive AMA, ultrasound shows no obstruction; biopsy only if the diagnosis is uncertain (portal lymphocytes, duct loss, granulomas in about 40%)
**PSC**: MRCP shows multifocal strictures with dilatation ('beading'); biopsy shows periductal **'onion-skin' fibrosis**; small-duct PSC can be missed on cholangiography
**Cholangiocarcinoma**: CT and MRI for diagnosis and staging; CA19-9 raised in up to 80% but also in benign obstruction; ERCP brush cytology or EUS-guided sampling for tissue
blocks.title: Diagnosing PBC, PSC and cholangiocarcinoma

blocks.note: MRCP in PSC: beaded, strictured and dilated intrahepatic ducts with a diffusely narrowed extrahepatic duct
PSC histology: concentric 'onion-skin' scarring around a bile duct
ERCP showing filling defects (stones) in the common bile duct
ERCP in cholangiocarcinoma: distal malignant stricture with dilated duct above, then a self-expanding metal stent across it
PBC histology: portal tract infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells

blocks.text: Diagnostic ERCP has been largely replaced by MRCP, which images the ducts as well and is safer. Choose ERCP when you expect to **treat** (stones, strictures, drainage).
Very high transaminases in a patient with RUQ pain do not always mean hepatitis - an impacted duct stone can cause a short-lived transaminase surge. Look for duct dilatation and the clinical picture.

Ultrasound is the **investigation of choice for gallstones**. Transabdominal scanning detects gallbladder stones with sensitivity above 92% and specificity of 99%, and it beats CT, MRCP and EUS for stones _inside the gallbladder_. Stones appear as echogenic foci casting an **acoustic shadow**. Scanning after a fast of at least 8 hours gives a distended, bile-filled gallbladder.

blocks.title: What ultrasound can and cannot do
rows: Stones (especially in the neck or cystic duct), wall thickening (>4 mm), pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign; PPV about 92% and NPV about 95% with a typical history
Dilated intra- and extrahepatic ducts show a mechanical cause; a CBD over about 6 mm suggests a duct stone
Poor - about half of duct stones are missed, especially in the distal CBD

blocks.note: Gallbladder stone with posterior acoustic shadow on ultrasound
Labelled ultrasound: liver, gallbladder, gallstone and its acoustic shadow
Acute cholecystitis: thickened gallbladder wall with a large stone

blocks.text: Ultrasound answers the key jaundice question - **are the ducts dilated?** If yes, the jaundice is obstructive and the next step is cholangiography (MRCP, or ERCP if treatment is needed).
A normal ultrasound does **not** exclude a bile duct stone: about 50% are missed. If suspicion persists (cholestatic LFTs, dilated duct, pancreatitis), proceed to MRCP or EUS.

Gallbladder wall thickening is non-specific: it also occurs with hypoalbuminaemia, portal hypertension and acute viral hepatitis. Look for stones and focal (sonographic) tenderness before calling it cholecystitis.

blocks.title: Autoantibody frequency (%) in chronic non-viral liver disease

items: **AMA** in over 95%, directed at the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex; it is diagnostic in the right setting
The **anti-M2** subtype is about 98% specific; the AMA titre does not track disease severity
PBC-specific ANAs (e.g. anti-**gp210**) stain the nuclear rim or nuclear dots - not the homogeneous ANA of autoimmune hepatitis; anti-gp210 (about 50%) predicts progression to liver failure
Immunoglobulin rise is typically **IgM** (IgG in autoimmune hepatitis)
AMA with normal LFTs is latent disease; a minority develop PBC over the following years
blocks.title: PBC serology

blocks.text: **AMA-negative PBC** ('autoimmune cholangitis') has the clinical, biochemical and histological picture of PBC without AMA; transaminases, immunoglobulins and ANA titres tend to be higher, but the course is the same. Without AMA, the diagnosis needs liver histology and cholangiography (usually MRCP) to exclude other duct disease.

items: **pANCA** in 60-80% of PSC, but also in 30-40% of UC alone and about 50% of autoimmune hepatitis - supportive, never diagnostic
Low-titre ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody in PSC have no diagnostic value; **AMA is absent**
**IgG4-associated cholangitis**: raised serum IgG4 and IgG4-positive plasma cells on biopsy; distinguishes a steroid-responsive mimic of PSC
blocks.title: PSC and IgG4 disease

blocks.text: Raised ALP + raised IgM + positive AMA makes PBC almost certain; biopsy adds staging but is not needed for the diagnosis.

AMA positivity in PBC is quoted as 90% (Davidson's comparison box), 95% (Davidson's antibody table) and over 95% (Davidson text). Exam answer: AMA is positive in **about 95%** - so a negative AMA does not exclude PBC.

blocks.title: Gallstones
rows: No treatment - most never cause symptoms
Consider cholecystectomy for porcelain gallbladder, polyps 10 mm or more, stones over 3 cm, haemolytic anaemia (e.g. sickle cell)
Cholecystectomy in the same admission; waiting for elective surgery risks recurrence (about 30% over 4 months)
Oral bile acids (ursodeoxycholic or chenodeoxycholic acid) - low dissolution rate and stones recur after stopping
NSAIDs first; opiates for severe pain

items: Bed rest, IV fluids, analgesia (NSAID, or opiate if severe), nil by mouth; nasogastric tube only for persistent vomiting
Antibiotics: a cephalosporin (e.g. cefuroxime) or piperacillin-tazobactam; add metronidazole if severely ill
Cholecystectomy **within 5 days** of onset; urgent surgery if it progresses or empyema/perforation develops
Too inflamed or unfit: percutaneous gallbladder drainage, then cholecystectomy 4-6 weeks later
Acalculous cholecystitis: early cholecystectomy, or percutaneous cholecystostomy if too ill
blocks.title: Acute cholecystitis

items: Blood cultures **before** antibiotics; IV fluids, analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. cefuroxime + metronidazole)
Urgent biliary decompression: **ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction** (about 90% success)
If ERCP fails: percutaneous transhepatic drainage, combined procedures, lithotripsy or surgery
Then remove the gallbladder (within about 6 weeks) to prevent recurrence
blocks.title: Cholangitis and bile duct stones
Primary biliary cholangitis
rows: **Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 13-15 mg/kg/day** for life - first line; improves LFTs and may slow progression
**Obeticholic acid** (FXR agonist); fibrates are an add-on option. Glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressants show no overall benefit (and steroids worsen bone loss)
Colestyramine 4-16 g/day, spaced from UDCA; then rifampicin, naltrexone, plasmapheresis or MARS
Calcium and vitamin D; bisphosphonate if osteoporotic
Replace fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, K); exclude coeliac disease
Liver transplant for liver failure or intractable itch; bilirubin is the best marker of decline (Kumar: persistently above 100 umol/L)

items: **PSC**: no curative drug; UDCA is widely used but evidence is limited
Cholangitis episodes: antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin
Dominant extrahepatic stricture: balloon dilatation or stenting at ERCP **after excluding cholangiocarcinoma**
Fat-soluble vitamins and bone protection; surveillance for cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer
Liver transplant for advanced disease (5-year survival 80-90%); PSC can recur in the graft; cholangiocarcinoma contraindicates transplant
**IgG4-associated cholangitis**: glucocorticoids
**Cholangiocarcinoma**: resection in only about 20%; most are palliated with an endoscopic or percutaneous stent
**Sphincter of Oddi**: sphincterotomy for organic stenosis but not for functional pain; nifedipine or low-dose amitriptyline may help; rectal diclofenac 100 mg reduces post-ERCP pancreatitis
blocks.title: PSC, IgG4 disease and others

blocks.text: Timing of cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis differs: Davidson says within 5 days, quick sources say within 24-48 hours, Kumar waits a few days but operates in the same admission. All agree: **early surgery in the index admission**; delaying 2-3 months is no longer favoured.

UDCA in PSC: Davidson notes wide use with limited evidence (possible colon cancer benefit); Kumar finds no proven benefit and warns that high-dose UDCA (30 mg/kg) may be harmful. Only liver transplantation changes the outlook.

In cholangitis, quick sources note that most patients settle on antibiotics and only about 20% need emergency ERCP, while Davidson stresses urgent decompression. A septic or deteriorating patient needs drainage now.

cards.front: Commonest disorder of the biliary tree?
cards.back: Gallstones (about 11% prevalence in adults in developed countries; commoner in women)

cards.front: Black versus brown pigment stones: composition and setting?
cards.back: Black: polymerised calcium bilirubinate - haemolysis, cirrhosis. Brown: calcium bilirubinate from infected, static bile - Far East, ducts

cards.front: Three mechanisms behind cholesterol gallstones?
cards.back: More cholesterol secreted, poor gallbladder emptying (stasis), less bile salt secreted

cards.front: PSC and ulcerative colitis: how often does each occur with the other?
cards.back: About two-thirds of PSC patients have UC; 3-10% of UC patients develop PSC

cards.front: Target antigen of antimitochondrial antibody in PBC?
cards.back: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (a mitochondrial enzyme)

cards.front: Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad?
cards.back: Triad: jaundice, fever, RUQ pain. Pentad adds shock and confusion

cards.front: Biliary pain lasting more than 6 hours suggests what?
cards.back: A complication: acute cholecystitis or pancreatitis

cards.front: Courvoisier's law?
cards.back: Palpable gallbladder + jaundice: gallstones unlikely; suspect malignant obstruction (e.g. pancreatic cancer)

cards.front: Mirizzi's syndrome?
cards.back: Stone impacted in the cystic duct compressing the common hepatic duct, causing obstructive jaundice; mimics malignant stricture

cards.front: In PBC, which symptoms usually come before jaundice?
cards.back: Fatigue and pruritus (often worst on the limbs); jaundice is late and fever does not occur

cards.front: Cholangiocarcinoma risk in PSC (Davidson)?
cards.back: About 10-30% over the disease course; lifetime risk about 20%

cards.front: LFT pattern of biliary obstruction?
cards.back: ALP markedly up (>5x), GGT moderately up (2-5x), AST/ALT mildly up (<2x)

cards.front: Amylase level that confidently attributes abdominal pain to acute pancreatitis?
cards.back: Above 1000 U/L

cards.front: Classic liver biopsy finding in PSC?
cards.back: Periductal 'onion-skin' fibrosis

cards.front: Sensitivity and specificity of transabdominal ultrasound for gallbladder stones?
cards.back: Sensitivity over 92%, specificity 99%

cards.front: What fraction of bile duct stones does ultrasound miss?
cards.back: About half, especially in the distal CBD

cards.front: How common is pANCA in PSC, and is it diagnostic?
cards.back: 60-80%; not diagnostic (also in UC alone and autoimmune hepatitis)

cards.front: Immunofluorescence pattern of PBC-specific ANA (e.g. anti-gp210)?
cards.back: Nuclear rim or nuclear dots - unlike the homogeneous ANA of autoimmune hepatitis

cards.front: First-line drug and dose for PBC?
cards.back: Ursodeoxycholic acid 13-15 mg/kg/day

cards.front: First-line treatment for cholestatic pruritus?
cards.back: Colestyramine 4-16 g/day, taken apart from UDCA

cards.front: Treatment of IgG4-associated cholangitis?
cards.back: Glucocorticoids - it responds well, unlike PSC

cards.front: Definitive treatment of cholangitis due to a CBD stone?
cards.back: Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction (about 90% success), after cultures and antibiotics

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had three episodes of RUQ pain with fevers since her teens. MRCP shows fusiform dilatation of the entire common bile duct with normal intrahepatic ducts and no stones.
items.explanation: Diffuse CBD dilatation in a young adult with recurrent pain and cholangitis is a type I choledochal cyst (the commonest type, about 87%). It carries a cholangiocarcinoma risk, so it is excised.

items.stem: A 77-year-old woman with known gallstones presents with vomiting and colicky abdominal distension. Plain film shows dilated small bowel loops and air in the biliary tree.
items.explanation: Pneumobilia plus small bowel obstruction means a stone has eroded through a cholecysto-enteric fistula and impacted in the bowel, usually the terminal ileum: gallstone ileus.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has deepening jaundice and RUQ discomfort. Ultrasound shows a stone impacted in the cystic duct and a dilated common hepatic duct above the cystic duct level, with a normal-calibre distal CBD.
items.explanation: Extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone lodged in the cystic duct is Mirizzi's syndrome. The key differential is a malignant hilar stricture.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely underlying cause from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Rapid weight loss after bariatric surgery

items.stem: A 15-year-old boy with lifelong mild jaundice, splenomegaly and a family history of splenectomy has biliary pain. Ultrasound shows several small gallbladder stones.
items.explanation: Black pigment stones in a teenager with chronic haemolysis (splenomegaly, family history, unconjugated jaundice) point to hereditary spherocytosis.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man who grew up in southern China has recurrent fevers, jaundice and RUQ pain. ERCP removes soft brown stones from dilated intrahepatic ducts; he had a cholecystectomy 10 years ago.
items.explanation: Brown pigment stones forming within the ducts from infected, static bile are typical of the Far East, where liver fluke infection such as Clonorchis sinensis triggers primary duct stones.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man with a low CD4 count has diarrhoea, RUQ pain and a raised ALP. MRCP shows irregular strictures of intra- and extrahepatic ducts. He has no inflammatory bowel disease.
items.explanation: Sclerosing cholangitis in advanced HIV without IBD is secondary sclerosing cholangitis, most likely from Cryptosporidium (or CMV) infection.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has had constant epigastric pain radiating to the tip of her right scapula for 9 hours. She is febrile (38.3 C) and tender under the right costal margin, with arrest of inspiration on palpation there. White cell count is 15 x 10^9/L; bilirubin is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pain lasting more than 6 hours with fever, leucocytosis and a positive Murphy's sign means inflammation of the gallbladder wall - acute cholecystitis. Normal bilirubin argues against duct obstruction.
whyNot: Biliary colic settles within a few hours and has no fever, leucocytosis or peritonism.
Cholangitis would usually bring jaundice (Charcot's triad); bilirubin is normal here.
A duct stone usually raises bilirubin and ALP; fever and a Murphy's sign point to the gallbladder.
Mirizzi's syndrome causes obstructive jaundice from common hepatic duct compression.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has 6 weeks of progressive painless jaundice, itch and weight loss. On examination there is a smooth, non-tender, palpable mass under the right costal margin that moves with respiration.
questions.leadIn: Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
questions.explanation: Courvoisier's law: a palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient makes gallstone obstruction unlikely, because a chronically inflamed stone-bearing gallbladder cannot distend. Progressive painless jaundice with weight loss suggests malignant distal obstruction, classically pancreatic cancer.
whyNot: Stone-related jaundice tends to fluctuate, follows pain, and the scarred gallbladder is usually impalpable.
PBC causes itch and later jaundice but no distended gallbladder; it typically affects women.
Mirizzi's syndrome is caused by a stone in a usually chronically inflamed gallbladder, which does not distend.
Hepatitis gives a hepatocellular picture and does not produce a palpable gallbladder.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has 2 years of tiredness and generalised itch, worse on her arms and legs, and gritty eyes with a dry mouth. ALP is 4 times normal, bilirubin normal. She has never had fever.
questions.leadIn: Which condition is she most likely to have?
questions.explanation: A middle-aged woman with fatigue and limb-predominant pruritus long before jaundice, cholestatic LFTs and sicca symptoms (Sjogren's) is the classic picture of PBC. Fever and rigors do not occur in PBC.
whyNot: PSC mainly affects younger men with ulcerative colitis.
Duct stones cause episodic pain and fluctuating jaundice, not years of itch.
Cholangiocarcinoma presents with obstructive jaundice, often with pain and weight loss, not years of itch with a normal bilirubin.
Cholangitis is an acute febrile illness.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with PSC and ulcerative colitis has been stable for 6 years. Over 2 months he has lost 5 kg and become jaundiced. MRCP shows a new tight stricture at the hilum on a background of beaded ducts.
questions.leadIn: Which complication must be excluded first?
questions.explanation: A new dominant stricture in PSC, especially with weight loss, must be treated as cholangiocarcinoma until proven otherwise (about 10-30% of PSC patients develop it). Do this before dilating or stenting the stricture.
whyNot: Stones can form in PSC, but weight loss and a new hilar stricture point to malignancy.
Cirrhosis is a diffuse process and does not explain a new focal stricture.
IgG4 disease is a PSC mimic, not a complication of established PSC.
Gallbladder carcinoma usually affects older women and does not present as a hilar duct stricture.

questions.theme: Choice of investigation in biliary disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely next investigation from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has an ALP persistently three times normal. Ultrasound shows no gallstones and no obvious duct dilatation. AMA is negative.
items.explanation: Suspected PSC: MRCP is the key, usually diagnostic, non-invasive test, showing multifocal strictures and beading. ERCP is kept for therapy.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has had four attacks of acute pancreatitis with no alcohol history. Repeated transabdominal ultrasound and MRCP are normal.
items.explanation: Recurrent unexplained pancreatitis may be due to microlithiasis in the gallbladder or CBD, which endoscopic ultrasound detects best.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man treated for 4 days for acute cholecystitis has worsening pain, a swinging fever and a rising white cell count. Ultrasound confirms stones and a thick-walled gallbladder.
items.explanation: Failure to settle raises concern about empyema or perforation; Davidson recommends CT to assess these complications rather than repeating ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has had two episodes of RUQ pain with transient jaundice. Bilirubin is 58 umol/L and ALP 3 times normal. Ultrasound shows gallbladder stones and a CBD of 9 mm, but no stone is seen within the duct.
questions.leadIn: What is the best interpretation of the ultrasound?
options: A bile duct stone is excluded
A duct stone is still likely; ultrasound misses about half of them
The dilatation must be due to a pancreatic tumour
The findings indicate primary sclerosing cholangitis
questions.explanation: Ultrasound misses about 50% of bile duct stones, particularly in the distal CBD. A dilated duct with fluctuating jaundice still points to choledocholithiasis; MRCP or EUS is the next step.
whyNot: Ultrasound is too insensitive for duct stones to exclude them.
Fluctuating jaundice after pain with gallbladder stones favours a stone over a tumour.
PSC shows strictures and beading on cholangiography, not a uniformly dilated CBD with stones.
Dilated ducts indicate an obstructive (post-hepatic) cause.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has typical intermittent episodes of epigastric pain after meals. LFTs are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is the best first test to confirm gallstones in the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: Transabdominal ultrasound is the investigation of choice: sensitivity above 92% and specificity 99% for gallbladder stones, and better than CT, MRCP or EUS for stones in the gallbladder.
whyNot: CT misses many stones that are not calcified.
MRCP is better for duct stones and is not first-line for gallbladder stones.
ERCP is invasive, carries a pancreatitis risk and is now used mainly for therapy on the ducts.
Plain films see only stones with enough calcium and are far less sensitive than ultrasound.

questions.theme: Serological markers in biliary and liver disease
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely test from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has itch and an ALP 5 times normal. Ultrasound shows undilated ducts. Serum IgM is raised. Which single antibody would confirm the likely diagnosis without a biopsy?
items.explanation: Cholestatic LFTs, raised IgM and normal ducts in a middle-aged woman suggest PBC; AMA is positive in about 95% and, with these findings, makes biopsy unnecessary.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man has painless obstructive jaundice. He has known autoimmune pancreatitis, and MRCP shows hilar and distal bile duct strictures resembling PSC.
items.explanation: Autoimmune pancreatitis with PSC-like strictures suggests IgG4-associated cholangitis; a raised serum IgG4 supports the diagnosis and predicts a good response to steroids.

items.stem: A woman with known AMA-positive PBC asks whether any antibody predicts a worse course. Which antibody, giving a nuclear rim pattern, is linked to progression to liver failure?
items.explanation: PBC-specific ANAs such as anti-gp210 give rim or dot nuclear staining; anti-gp210 (in about half) correlates with progression. AMA titre does not reflect severity.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has PBC confirmed by cholestatic LFTs and a positive AMA. She has mild itch and no cirrhosis.
questions.leadIn: What is the first-line disease-modifying treatment?
questions.explanation: UDCA (13-15 mg/kg/day) is the optimal first-line therapy for PBC: it improves LFTs and may slow histological progression. It is lifelong.
whyNot: Glucocorticoids show no overall benefit in PBC and worsen bone loss.
Obeticholic acid is second line, for inadequate response to UDCA.
Immunosuppressants have not shown overall benefit in PBC.
Colestyramine treats itch but does not modify the disease.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man has rigors, jaundice and RUQ pain. BP is 96/60 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a dilated CBD and gallbladder stones. Blood cultures have been taken and IV fluids and cefuroxime with metronidazole started.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction
questions.explanation: Acute cholangitis from a duct stone needs urgent biliary decompression. ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction is the treatment of choice and succeeds in about 90%; percutaneous drainage is the fallback.
whyNot: Cholecystectomy does not drain the obstructed bile duct and is risky in a septic patient.
Bile acid dissolution is slow and has no role in septic obstruction.
Delaying drainage in a hypotensive patient risks death from biliary sepsis.
HIDA assesses cystic duct patency for cholecystitis and adds nothing here.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man on ICU for 2 weeks after major burns, fed parenterally, develops fever and RUQ tenderness. Ultrasound shows a distended, thick-walled gallbladder with no stones.
items.explanation: Gallbladder inflammation without stones in a critically ill, parenterally fed patient is acalculous cholecystitis, caused by stasis and ischaemia.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting and amylase of 2400 U/L. Ultrasound shows small gallbladder stones; she drinks no alcohol.
items.explanation: Amylase above 1000 U/L confidently attributes the pain to pancreatitis; small stones passing through the ampulla are the usual cause.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with diabetes has RUQ pain and sepsis. Plain film shows gas outlining the gallbladder wall.
items.explanation: Gas in the gallbladder wall from gas-forming organisms in an elderly diabetic is emphysematous cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman complains of bloating, belching and fatty-food intolerance for a year with no discrete pain attacks. Ultrasound incidentally shows two small gallbladder stones.
items.explanation: Fatty food intolerance, flatulence and dyspepsia are not caused by gallstones; they are best regarded as functional dyspepsia, and the stones are incidental.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely management from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission
Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction
ERCP balloon dilatation or stenting of a stricture
Endoscopic sphincterotomy for organic sphincter stenosis

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has gallstones seen on an ultrasound done for renal colic. He has never had abdominal pain and his LFTs are normal.
items.explanation: Incidental asymptomatic gallstones should not be treated because most never cause symptoms.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman with PBC has taken UDCA at full dose for over a year; her ALP remains 3 times normal. She has compensated liver disease.
items.explanation: Inadequate response to UDCA is the indication for obeticholic acid, an FXR agonist (avoid in decompensated cirrhosis).

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with IgG4-associated cholangitis and autoimmune pancreatitis has obstructive jaundice. Cholangiocarcinoma has been excluded.
items.explanation: IgG4-associated cholangitis responds well to glucocorticoids, unlike PSC.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with PBC has a bilirubin persistently above 100 umol/L and new ascites despite UDCA.
items.explanation: Liver failure in PBC is the indication for transplantation; bilirubin is the most reliable marker of decline, and Kumar uses a persistent level above 100 umol/L.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman is admitted with her second attack of gallstone-related acute cholecystitis. After 2 days of IV antibiotics she is pain-free and eating.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate plan?
questions.explanation: Early cholecystectomy in the index admission (Davidson: within 5 days of onset) is preferred; delaying 2-3 months is no longer favoured because attacks recur often if the gallbladder stays.
whyNot: With the gallbladder left in place, further colic or cholecystitis is common.
Bile acid dissolution has a low success rate and stones recur after stopping.
Waiting carries a high recurrence risk (about 30% over 4 months for pain).
ERCP treats duct stones; there is no evidence of a CBD stone here.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has 3 days of jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. ALP is 7 times normal, GGT 4 times, ALT 1.5 times. Ultrasound shows dilated intra- and extrahepatic ducts with no visible cause.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: **Step 1 - pattern:** ALP over 5x with GGT 2-5x and only mild ALT rise is a cholestatic (obstructive) pattern. **Step 2 - ultrasound:** dilated ducts mean the obstruction is mechanical and extrahepatic. **Step 3 - next test:** the jaundice algorithm moves to cholangiography; MRCP is preferred as it is as good as ERCP for imaging and safer, with ERCP kept for therapy once the cause is known.
whyNot: Biopsy is for hepatocellular or intrahepatic disease and is risky with large duct obstruction (biliary peritonitis).
Serology and autoantibodies are for hepatocellular jaundice without duct dilatation.
HIDA assesses gallbladder filling in suspected cholecystitis, not the cause of duct obstruction.
Obstructive jaundice needs prompt imaging of the cause.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has 6 hours of severe RUQ pain. ALT is 780 U/L (AST 410 U/L), ALP twice normal, bilirubin 42 umol/L. The next morning ALT has fallen to 260 U/L. Ultrasound shows gallbladder stones and a CBD of 8 mm.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Step 1:** A transaminase spike with RUQ pain could look hepatitic. **Step 2:** Rapid fall over 24 hours, ALT greater than AST, gallstones and a dilated CBD fit a stone impacting and then passing; complete duct obstruction can raise transaminases 10-15 times. **Step 3:** Confirm with MRCP/EUS and clear the duct.
whyNot: Viral hepatitis gives a hepatocellular picture without a dilated CBD; a spike that falls within a day fits a passing stone.
Autoimmune hepatitis brings raised IgG and autoantibodies and does not dilate the CBD.
Hepatic ischaemia is a cause of ALT above 1000 U/L; nothing here suggests it, and it would not dilate the CBD.
PBC causes a slowly rising ALP with undilated ducts.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman has itch and a cholestatic LFT picture. Ultrasound is normal. AMA is negative, ANA is high titre, transaminases are moderately raised, and biopsy shows bile duct destruction with granulomas. MRCP is normal.
items.explanation: Step 1: cholestasis with normal ducts suggests intrahepatic disease. Step 2: PBC histology without AMA, with high ANA and higher transaminases, is AMA-negative PBC. Step 3: Davidson requires biopsy plus MRCP when AMA is absent; the course mirrors classic PBC.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has AMA-positive cholestasis but also ALT 8 times normal, high IgG and interface hepatitis on biopsy.
items.explanation: Step 1: AMA and cholestatic LFTs point to PBC. Step 2: marked transaminases, high immunoglobulins and interface hepatitis add autoimmune hepatitis. This overlap may benefit from a trial of glucocorticoids.

items.stem: A 65-year-old man had a bile duct injury at cholecystectomy 8 years ago with repeated cholangitis since. He now has splenomegaly and ascites; MRCP shows a tight benign stricture with upstream dilatation.
items.explanation: Step 1: years of large-duct obstruction and cholangitis. Step 2: portal hypertension features mean cirrhosis has developed. A benign stricture causing long-standing obstruction leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely explanation of the findings from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Gallbladder wall oedema from portal hypertension or hypoalbuminaemia

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has a thickened (6 mm) gallbladder wall on routine ultrasound. There are no stones, no focal tenderness and he is afebrile.
items.explanation: Wall thickening is non-specific: hypoalbuminaemia, portal hypertension and acute hepatitis cause it. Without stones or sonographic Murphy's sign, cholecystitis is unlikely.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman with fever and RUQ pain has a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck, a 5 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and maximal tenderness when the probe presses over the gallbladder.
items.explanation: Stone in the neck, wall over 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid and a sonographic Murphy's sign together indicate acute calculous cholecystitis.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has painless jaundice. Ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic ducts in both lobes but a normal-calibre CBD.
items.explanation: Dilated intrahepatic ducts with a normal-calibre CBD place the block at the hilum, the commonest site (50-60%) of cholangiocarcinoma.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman's ultrasound for dyspepsia shows a 12 mm fixed, non-shadowing lesion projecting from the gallbladder wall.
items.explanation: A non-shadowing, fixed lesion is a polyp rather than a stone; at 10 mm or more it warrants cholecystectomy because of malignant potential.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has had three self-limiting episodes of itch followed by painless jaundice, each lasting about 2 months. Between episodes LFTs and liver biopsy are normal.
items.explanation: Recurrent cholestatic episodes from adolescence with a normal liver between attacks is benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis (ATP8B1/FIC1 mutations); prognosis is good.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man with pancolitis has fatigue and an ALP 4 times normal. pANCA is positive and AMA is negative. MRCP shows beaded intra- and extrahepatic ducts.
items.explanation: Young man, ulcerative colitis, cholestasis, pANCA and beading on MRCP: primary sclerosing cholangitis.

items.stem: A 76-year-old woman with long-standing gallstones has 2 months of weight loss and persistent jaundice. A firm RUQ mass is palpable and a plain film shows a calcified gallbladder wall.
items.explanation: Elderly woman with gallstones, a porcelain gallbladder, mass, weight loss and jaundice: carcinoma of the gallbladder.

items.stem: A 42-year-old man from South-east Asia has repeated attacks of fever, upper abdominal pain and jaundice. Imaging shows intra- and extrahepatic ducts packed with soft pigment sludge and stones, with liver abscesses.
items.explanation: Intrahepatic duct sludge and calcium bilirubinate stones with secondary infection in a South-east Asian patient is recurrent pyogenic cholangitis.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with PBC on UDCA has severe itch that disturbs her sleep. Her doctor starts colestyramine.
questions.leadIn: Which advice about taking colestyramine is most important?
options: Take it at the same time as UDCA
Space it from UDCA, as it binds other drugs in the gut
Take it with a fatty meal to increase absorption
questions.explanation: Colestyramine (4-16 g/day) is first-line for cholestatic itch, but as an anion-binding resin it binds other drugs, most obviously UDCA, so doses must be spaced (quick sources: UDCA 2-4 hours apart).
whyNot: Taking them together means colestyramine binds UDCA.
The main dose is usually given around breakfast, when duodenal bile acids peak.
UDCA is lifelong disease therapy and should continue.
Colestyramine works by binding pruritogens inside the gut; a fatty meal plays no part in its use.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has RUQ pain for 12 hours. Amylase is 420 U/L (normal under 100), WBC 14 x 10^9/L, Murphy's sign positive. Ultrasound shows gallbladder stones and a thick wall.
questions.leadIn: How should the raised amylase be interpreted?
options: It is a moderate rise that can occur with other acute abdominal causes
questions.explanation: Moderately raised amylase occurs with many causes of abdominal pain, including cholecystitis. Only a level above 1000 U/L confidently attributes pain to acute pancreatitis.
whyNot: A moderate rise is not specific enough to confirm pancreatitis.
Nothing here suggests perforation; a plain film would help exclude it.
Parotitis is irrelevant in this clinical picture.
Cholecystitis can itself cause a mild amylase rise.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has PSC confirmed on MRCP. He asks about long-term treatment.
questions.leadIn: Which statement is most accurate?
options: No drug is proven to cure PSC; transplantation is the only definitive treatment for advanced disease
Antibiotics should be given long-term to prevent cholangitis
questions.explanation: There is no cure for PSC. UDCA is widely used but evidence is limited; immunosuppressants have been disappointing. Liver transplantation is the option for advanced disease, with good 5-year survival.
whyNot: Colectomy for UC does not change the course of PSC.
Immunosuppressants, including steroids, have given disappointing results in PSC.
Obeticholic acid is a second-line drug for PBC.
Antibiotics treat acute cholangitis but have no proven preventive value.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely drug from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman with PBC has a DEXA T-score of -2.8 at the hip. She already takes calcium and vitamin D.
items.explanation: Osteoporosis in PBC is treated with a bisphosphonate on top of calcium and vitamin D.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with obstructive jaundice from a CBD stone has an INR of 2.1 before planned ERCP. Liver synthetic function was previously normal.
items.explanation: Prolonged PT in biliary obstruction reflects vitamin K malabsorption and corrects with parenteral vitamin K, unlike PT prolongation from liver failure.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman is about to undergo ERCP and sphincterotomy for organic sphincter of Oddi stenosis. Which agent is recommended to lower the risk of procedure-related pancreatitis?
items.explanation: Prophylactic rectal NSAID (diclofenac 100 mg) reduces post-ERCP pancreatitis and has replaced routine pancreatic stenting.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a raised ALP and itch. AMA is negative on two occasions. Ultrasound shows normal ducts.
questions.leadIn: Before diagnosing PBC, what does Davidson recommend?
options: Start UDCA and recheck AMA in a year
No further tests; diagnose AMA-negative PBC clinically
questions.explanation: When AMA is absent, PBC should not be diagnosed without histology, and cholangiography (typically MRCP) is needed to exclude other biliary disease such as PSC.
whyNot: Treating without a diagnosis risks missing other cholestatic disease.
ERCP is invasive and reserved for therapy.
HIDA is a test for acute cholecystitis.
AMA-negative PBC still needs histological support.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the single most likely diagnosis from the list. Any option can be the answer for one patient, several patients or none.
options: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has intermittent jaundice, anaemia, vomiting and weight loss. Duodenal endoscopy shows an ulcerated mass at the papilla.
items.explanation: Anaemia and weight loss with intermittent jaundice and a mass at the papilla is ampullary carcinoma, diagnosed by duodenal endoscopy and biopsy.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man from northern Thailand has painless jaundice and weight loss. CA19-9 is raised. MRCP shows a hilar stricture with dilated intrahepatic ducts and a normal CBD.
items.explanation: Chronic liver fluke infection is a major cholangiocarcinoma risk in north Thailand; a hilar stricture with intrahepatic dilatation is the commonest pattern.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has obstructive jaundice and a hilar stricture. Serum IgG4 is high, he has autoimmune pancreatitis, and the stricture resolves after 6 weeks of prednisolone.
items.explanation: A steroid-responsive hilar stricture with raised IgG4 and autoimmune pancreatitis is IgG4-associated cholangitis, the key mimic of cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman has RUQ pain and a fever for 3 days, treated as acute cholecystitis. She remains unwell with a tender RUQ mass. She is considered too frail for surgery because of severe heart failure.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation: When cholecystectomy is too risky or technically difficult, percutaneous gallbladder drainage controls the sepsis; interval cholecystectomy can follow 4-6 weeks later if she becomes fit.
whyNot: Her comorbidity makes emergency surgery dangerous.
Bile acids are slow and do not treat an infected gallbladder.
ERCP drains the bile duct, not an obstructed gallbladder.
Lithotripsy is reserved for a few selected gallbladder stones with a patent cystic duct; it does not drain an infected gallbladder.

ospe.identify: Ultrasound: echogenic gallstone in the gallbladder with a posterior acoustic shadow - cholelithiasis
Ultrasound: thickened gallbladder wall around a large stone - acute calculous cholecystitis
MRCP: multifocal strictures and dilatations ('beading') of intrahepatic ducts with a narrowed extrahepatic duct - primary sclerosing cholangitis
Liver histology: concentric periductal 'onion-skin' fibrosis - primary sclerosing cholangitis
ERCP: filling defects within the common bile duct - choledocholithiasis
ERCP: tight distal bile duct stricture with upstream dilatation (cholangiocarcinoma), then a self-expanding metal stent placed across it
Liver histology: portal tract infiltrate of lymphocytes and plasma cells - primary biliary cholangitis
Imaging: thin rim of calcification outlining the gallbladder wall - porcelain gallbladder (cancer risk; cholecystectomy advised)
